title: Portitor Charon. Umbrae insepultae. Palinurus
titleEn: Charon, the Unburied and Palinurus — Aeneid VI.295–397
about: From the entrance a road leads down to Acheron, a seething flood that pours its sand into Cocytus. Its ferryman is Charon, a filthy old man with an unkempt white beard and eyes of fire, who poles and sails his dark boat across, old but with a god's green strength. To the bank streams a whole crowd of the dead, mothers and men, heroes, boys and unmarried girls, young men burned before their parents' eyes, as many as the leaves that fall in the first frost of autumn or the birds that flock to land when winter drives them over the sea. They stand and stretch out their hands in longing for the farther shore, but Charon takes some and drives others back. Aeneas asks why, and the Sibyl explains: these are the unburied, who must wander a hundred years along the bank before they may cross; those in the boat have had their burial. Among them Aeneas sees Leucaspis and Orontes, lost with their ship in the storm of Book I, and then his helmsman Palinurus, who fell overboard on the voyage to Italy. Aeneas asks which god drowned him, since Apollo had promised he would come safe to Italy. Palinurus answers that no god drowned him: he fell with the rudder torn away, drifted three nights, reached the Italian coast, and was killed there by savage people who took him for plunder; his body still lies tossed by the waves. He begs Aeneas to bury him or take him across the river. The Sibyl rebukes the wish, since the unburied may not cross and prayers do not bend fate, but comforts him: the neighbouring peoples, driven by portents, will give his bones a tomb and yearly rites, and the place will bear his name for ever. Aeneas and the Sibyl go on to the river, and Charon, seeing an armed man, shouts at him to halt and say why he has come: this is the realm of shades, and living bodies may not ride in his boat; he had no joy of carrying Hercules, who dragged off the watchdog of Hell, or Theseus and Pirithous, who tried to carry off the queen of the dead.

sentences.t: Hinc via, Tartarei quae fert Acherontis ad undas.
sentences.l: From here the road, which leads to Tartarean Acheron's waters.
sentences.i: From here a road runs down to the waters of Acheron in the depths of Tartarus.
sentences.n: A new paragraph. The verb is left out: 'hinc via (est)', 'from here (there is) the road'. 'Quae' stands second in its clause, after 'Tartarei', which is put first for weight; 'Tartarei… Acherontis' frames the relative clause. 'Fert' is 'carries', 'leads', as a road leads somewhere. Acheron, 'the river of woe', is one of the rivers of the underworld in Homer's Odyssey (10.513), with Cocytus, 'the river of wailing', flowing into it; Tartarus is the deep pit of the underworld, and 'Tartareus' here means simply 'of the world below'.

sentences.t:
Turbidus hic caeno vastaque voragine gurges
aestuat, atque omnem Cocyto eructat harenam.
sentences.l:
Turbid here with mud and with vast whirlpool a flood
seethes, and all into Cocytus belches its sand.
sentences.i: Here a flood thick with mud boils in a vast whirling gulf and spews all its sand into Cocytus.
sentences.n: 'Turbidus… gurges' frames the line, 'a muddy flood', the stream of Acheron. 'Caeno vastaque voragine' are ablatives of description, 'with mud and a huge whirlpool'. 'Aestuat' is 'seethes', 'boils', as the sea does in a swell. 'Cocyto' is a dative of direction, 'into Cocytus', a usage of verse. 'Eructat' is 'belches out', a coarse, vivid word. 'Omnem… harenam' is 'all its sand'. Virgil's rivers of the dead run into one another, and he does not keep their geography sharp: the stream Charon crosses is called by turns Acheron, Cocytus (323) and the Styx (385).

sentences.i: A fearful ferryman keeps these waters and streams, Charon, terrible in his squalor; a thick grey beard lies untended on his chin;
sentences.n: 'Portitor' is 'ferryman' (the same word means a collector of harbour dues), and his name is held back to the start of the next line, 'Charon'. 'Horrendus' goes with 'portitor', 'dreadful'. 'Servat' is 'watches over', 'keeps'. 'Terribili squalore' is an ablative of description, 'of terrible filth'. 'Cui… mento' is 'to whom… on the chin', a dative of reference standing for a possessive, 'on whose chin'; 'mento' is an ablative of place. 'Canities' is 'greyness', 'grey hair', here his beard, and 'plurima' is 'very abundant'. Charon is not in Homer; the old ferryman of the dead comes from later Greek belief, art and drama (he has a speaking part in Aristophanes' Frogs).

sentences.t:
stant lumina flamma,
sordidus ex umeris nodo dependet amictus.
sentences.l:
stand fixed his eyes with flame,
a filthy from his shoulders by a knot hangs cloak.
sentences.i: his eyes are fixed and blazing, and a filthy cloak hangs from his shoulders by a knot.
sentences.n: 'Stant lumina flamma' is 'his eyes stand with flame', that is, they stare, unmoving and fiery; 'lumina', 'lights', is the poetic word for eyes, and 'flamma' is an ablative of description or of means. 'Sordidus… amictus' frames the line, 'a dirty cloak'; 'nodo' is 'by a knot', knotted on the shoulder rather than pinned with a brooch, the dress of a working man. 'Dependet' is 'hangs down'. The two clauses stand side by side with no 'and'.

sentences.t:
Ipse ratem conto subigit, velisque ministrat,
et ferruginea subvectat corpora cymba,
iam senior, sed cruda deo viridisque senectus.
sentences.l:
He himself the boat with a pole pushes on, and to the sails attends,
and in his rust-dark ferries over bodies boat,
now rather old, but fresh to a god and green is old age.
sentences.i: He drives the boat on with a pole himself and tends the sails, and ferries the dead across in his dusky craft; he is old now, but a god's old age is hardy and green.
sentences.n: 'Ipse' is 'himself', with no crew. 'Conto subigit' is 'drives on with a pole', a punt-pole; 'velis ministrat' is 'serves the sails', 'velis' a dative. 'Ferruginea… cymba' frames the line, 'in a rust-coloured boat', that is dark, dusky; Greenough spells 'cymba', the Latin Library 'cumba'. 'Subvectat' is a frequentative of 'subveho', 'keeps carrying across'. 'Corpora' is 'bodies', though they are shades: Virgil keeps the word of the living world. 'Iam senior' is 'now elderly', the comparative meaning 'rather old'. In 'cruda deo viridisque senectus' the verb 'est' is left out; 'deo' is a dative of reference, 'for a god'; 'cruda' is 'raw', that is unripe, vigorous, and 'viridis' is 'green', still fresh.

sentences.t:
Huc omnis turba ad ripas effusa ruebat,
matres atque viri, defunctaque corpora vita
magnanimum heroum, pueri innuptaeque puellae,
impositique rogis iuvenes ante ora parentum:
sentences.l:
Here the whole crowd to the banks poured out was rushing,
mothers and men, and bodies having done with life
of great-souled heroes, boys and unwedded girls,
and young men placed on pyres before the faces of their parents:
sentences.i: Hither the whole throng came streaming and rushing to the banks, mothers and men, the lifeless bodies of great-hearted heroes, boys and unmarried girls, and young men laid on the pyre before their parents' eyes:
sentences.n: A new paragraph. 'Huc' is 'to this place'. 'Effusa ruebat' is 'poured out, was rushing', the imperfect of a continuing scene. 'Defuncta… corpora vita' is 'bodies that have done with life': 'defungor', 'finish with', takes the ablative, 'vita'. 'Magnanimum heroum' has the old genitive plural in '-um' for 'magnanimorum', as so often. 'Innuptae' is 'unmarried'. 'Impositi rogis' is 'placed on pyres'; 'ante ora parentum' is 'before the faces of their parents', the worst of deaths, the young buried by the old. Lines 306–308 are repeated word for word from Virgil's own Georgics (4.475–477), where the dead flock to hear Orpheus; the list of brides, youths and old men who throng round Odysseus in Odyssey 11 (36–41) stands behind both.

sentences.t:
quam multa in silvis autumni frigore primo
lapsa cadunt folia, aut ad terram gurgite ab alto
quam multae glomerantur aves, ubi frigidus annus
trans pontum fugat, et terris immittit apricis.
sentences.l:
as many as in the woods at autumn's first cold
having slipped fall the leaves, or as to the land from the deep gulf
as many flock together birds, when the cold year
across the sea drives them, and sends them into sunny lands.
sentences.i: as many as the leaves that loosen and fall in the woods at the first chill of autumn, or as the birds that flock to land from the deep sea when the cold season drives them over the water and sends them to sunny countries.
sentences.n: A double simile, both halves opened by 'quam multa… quam multae', 'as many as'. 'Autumni frigore primo' is 'at the first cold of autumn', an ablative of time. 'Lapsa cadunt' is 'having slipped, they fall', the participle of the deponent 'labor'. 'Gurgite ab alto' is 'from the deep sea'; 'glomerantur' is 'gather in a mass', a passive with middle sense, 'flock'. 'Frigidus annus' is 'the cold part of the year', winter; 'fugat' and 'immittit' have the birds as their unstated object, and 'terris… apricis' is a dative of direction, 'into sunny lands'. Homer compares the generations of men to leaves (Iliad 6.146) and an army to flocks of migrating cranes (Iliad 3.3–5); Virgil turns both to the numberless dead.

sentences.t:
Stabant orantes primi transmittere cursum,
tendebantque manus ripae ulterioris amore.
sentences.l:
They stood begging first to make the crossing,
and they were stretching their hands in longing for the farther bank.
sentences.i: There they stood, pleading to be the first to cross, and stretched out their hands in longing for the farther shore.
sentences.n: 'Orantes… transmittere' is 'begging to cross', 'oro' with an infinitive, a construction of verse ('ut' with the subjunctive would be usual in prose). 'Primi' is predicative, 'to be first to make the crossing'. 'Transmittere cursum' is 'to send their course across', to cross. 'Ripae ulterioris amore' is 'with love of the farther bank', 'ripae' an objective genitive. The second line has been admired in every age for what its slow spondees and its gesture say without comment.

sentences.t:
Navita sed tristis nunc hos nunc accipit illos,
ast alios longe submotos arcet harena.
sentences.l:
The boatman, but grim, now these now takes those,
but others, far driven back, he keeps from the sand.
sentences.i: But the grim boatman takes now these, now those, and keeps others driven far off from the strand.
sentences.n: 'Navita' is the old and poetic form of 'nauta', 'sailor', here Charon. 'Sed' stands second in its clause, as it often does in verse. 'Tristis' is 'grim', 'stern'. 'Nunc hos nunc… illos' is 'now these, now those'. 'Ast' is an archaic form of 'at', 'but', kept in solemn verse. 'Longe submotos' is 'moved far back' ('summotos' in the Latin Library, the same word): 'summovere' is the word for a lictor clearing a crowd from a magistrate's path. 'Harena' is an ablative of separation with 'arcet', 'keeps away from the sand' of the shore.

sentences.t:
Aeneas, miratus enim motusque tumultu,
“Dic ait O virgo, quid volt concursus ad amnem?
sentences.l:
Aeneas, for he was wondering and stirred by the tumult,
“Tell me,” he says, “O maiden, what means the crowding to the river?
sentences.i: Aeneas, amazed and moved by the uproar, said: “Tell me, maiden, what does this thronging to the river mean?
sentences.n: A new paragraph. 'Enim' here is not quite 'for' at the start of a clause: put inside the phrase, it gives the reason for what follows, 'Aeneas (for he was amazed and moved by the commotion) says'. 'Miratus' is the perfect participle of the deponent 'miror', with present sense; 'tumultu' goes with both participles. The opening mark begins Aeneas's question, which runs to 320; the print sets no marks round 'ait', 'he says', as Greenough often does not. 'Dic' is the short imperative of 'dico'. 'O virgo' is the Sibyl, a virgin priestess of Apollo. 'Volt' is Greenough's old spelling of 'vult' (the Latin Library prints 'vult'), and 'quid volt' is 'what does it mean?', 'what is the point of it?'. 'Concursus' is 'a running together'.

sentences.t:
Quidve petunt animae, vel quo discrimine ripas
hae linquunt, illae remis vada livida verrunt?”
sentences.l:
Or what do they seek, the souls, or by what distinction the banks
these leave, those with oars the waters livid sweep?”
sentences.i: What are the souls asking for? And by what rule do these turn away from the shore, while those sweep the leaden waters with the oars?”
sentences.n: 'Quidve' is 'quid' with '-ve', 'or what?'. 'Quo discrimine' is 'by what distinction', what decides who crosses. 'Hae… illae' is 'these… those', set against each other with no 'and' (asyndeton): some leave the banks, that is turn back from them, while others are rowed across. 'Remis' is 'with oars', an ablative of means; 'vada' are properly 'shallows', here the waters; 'livida' is 'bluish-grey', 'leaden', the colour of a bruise. 'Verrunt' is 'sweep'. The closing mark ends the question.

sentences.t: Olli sic breviter fata est longaeva sacerdos:
sentences.l: To him thus briefly spoke the long-lived priestess:
sentences.i: The aged priestess answered him briefly:
sentences.n: 'Olli' is Greenough's old form of 'illi', 'to him', a dative, kept in epic for its archaic ring. 'Fata est' is the perfect of the deponent 'for', 'speak'. 'Longaeva' is 'long-lived': the Sibyl of Cumae was said to have been granted as many years as the grains of sand she could hold in her hand, and so to have lived on for centuries. The colon opens her answer.

sentences.t:
“Anchisa generate, deum certissima proles,
Cocyti stagna alta vides Stygiamque paludem,
di cuius iurare timent et fallere numen.
sentences.l:
“From Anchises born, of the gods most certain offspring,
Cocytus's pools deep you see and the Stygian marsh,
which the gods to swear by fear and to break the divinity.
sentences.i: “Son of Anchises, born beyond all doubt of the gods, you are looking on the deep pools of Cocytus and the marsh of Styx, by whose power the gods dread to swear and then to break their word.
sentences.n: The opening mark begins the Sibyl's answer, which runs to 330. 'Anchisa generate' is a vocative of the perfect participle of 'genero', 'begotten', with 'Anchisa', an ablative of origin from the Greek name 'Anchises', 'begotten of Anchises'. 'Deum' is the genitive plural in '-um' again, 'of the gods', and 'certissima proles' is 'most sure offspring', since his mother is Venus. 'Cocyti stagna alta' and 'Stygiam paludem' are the pools of Cocytus and the marsh of the Styx, treated as one water. 'Di cuius… timent' is 'whose divinity the gods fear', with 'cuius' (referring to the marsh) set late in its clause; 'iurare numen' is 'to swear by its power', 'iuro' with the accusative of what is sworn by, and 'fallere' is 'to break faith with' it. The gods' oath by the Styx is the most binding of all, in Homer (Iliad 15.37–38) and Hesiod (Theogony 775–806), where a god who forswears it lies breathless for a year.

sentences.t:
Haec omnis, quam cernis, inops inhumataque turba est;
portitor ille Charon; hi, quos vehit unda, sepulti.
sentences.l:
This whole, which you see, a helpless and unburied crowd is;
the ferryman that one is Charon; these, whom the wave carries, the buried.
sentences.i: All this crowd you see are the helpless and unburied; that ferryman is Charon; those the water carries are the buried.
sentences.n: 'Haec omnis… turba' frames the line, with the relative clause 'quam cernis', 'which you see', set inside it. 'Inops' is 'without resources', helpless, and 'inhumata' is 'unburied', from 'humus', 'earth'. In the last two clauses 'est' and 'sunt' are left out: 'portitor ille (est) Charon', 'hi… sepulti (sunt)'. 'Unda' is 'the wave', the river that bears the boat. Three clauses, three answers to Aeneas's three questions.

sentences.t:
Nec ripas datur horrendas et rauca fluenta
transportare prius quam sedibus ossa quierunt.
sentences.l:
Nor the banks is it granted, dreadful, and the hoarse streams
to carry them across, before in a resting-place the bones have found rest.
sentences.i: Nor may they be carried over the fearful banks and the roaring flood until their bones have come to rest in a grave.
sentences.n: 'Nec… datur' is 'nor is it granted', impersonal, with 'transportare' as its subject. 'Transportare' is 'to carry across', and like other verbs compounded with 'trans' it takes an accusative of the thing crossed, 'ripas… et rauca fluenta', 'across the banks and hoarse streams'; the persons carried, 'them', are left unstated. 'Rauca' is 'hoarse', 'roaring'. 'Prius quam' is 'priusquam', 'before', written as two words; with the perfect indicative 'quierunt' it states a plain fact of time. 'Quierunt' is the shortened perfect of 'quiesco' for 'quieverunt', 'have come to rest'. 'Sedibus' is 'in a dwelling', an ablative of place, the tomb. 'Ossa' are 'bones', the remains.

sentences.t:
Centum errant annos volitantque haec litora circum;
tum demum admissi stagna exoptata revisunt.”
sentences.l:
A hundred they wander years, and flit these shores around;
then at last admitted, the pools longed-for they visit again.”
sentences.i: For a hundred years they wander and flutter round these shores; only then are they let in, and come at last to the waters they have yearned for.”
sentences.n: 'Centum… annos' is an accusative of duration of time, 'for a hundred years'. 'Volitant' is 'flit', the frequentative of 'volo', 'fly', the restless movement of a shade. 'Haec litora circum' puts the preposition after its noun, 'round these shores'. 'Tum demum' is 'then and only then'. 'Admissi' is 'admitted', allowed on board. 'Exoptata' is 'longed-for'; 'revisunt' is 'visit again' or simply 'come to see': the 're-' may mean they come back to the bank they had to leave. The closing mark ends the Sibyl's answer. Behind the whole idea is Patroclus's ghost in Iliad 23 (71–74), begging Achilles for burial because the shades will not let him cross the river.

sentences.t:
Constitit Anchisa satus et vestigia pressit,
multa putans, sortemque animo miseratus iniquam.
sentences.l:
Halted the son of Anchises and his footsteps checked,
many things pondering, and their lot in his heart pitying, unjust.
sentences.i: The son of Anchises stood still and checked his steps, thinking long and pitying in his heart their unjust lot.
sentences.n: 'Anchisa satus' is 'sprung from Anchises', 'satus' from 'sero', 'sow', 'beget', with 'Anchisa' again an ablative of origin; it is a stately name for Aeneas. 'Constitit' is 'stood still', and 'vestigia pressit' is 'checked his steps', as at 197. 'Multa putans' is 'thinking over many things'. 'Sortem… iniquam' frames the end of the line, 'the unequal lot', unjust because it falls on the dead through no fault of their own. 'Miseratus' is the participle of the deponent 'miseror', 'pity', and 'animo' is 'in his heart'.

sentences.t:
Cernit ibi maestos et mortis honore carentes
Leucaspim et Lyciae ductorem classis Oronten,
quos, simul ab Troia ventosa per aequora vectos,
obruit Auster, aqua involvens navemque virosque.
sentences.l:
He sees there, sad and of death's honour lacking,
Leucaspis and of Lycia's the leader fleet, Orontes,
whom, together from Troy over the windy seas carried,
overwhelmed the South Wind, in water rolling up both ship and men.
sentences.i: There he saw, sorrowing and denied the honours of the dead, Leucaspis and Orontes, captain of the Lycian ships, who had sailed with him from Troy over the windy seas until the South Wind overwhelmed them and swallowed ship and crew alike.
sentences.n: 'Cernit' is a historic present. 'Mortis honore carentes' is 'lacking the honour of death', funeral rites; 'careo' takes the ablative. 'Leucaspim' and 'Oronten' are Greek accusatives. Orontes and his Lycian ship were sunk before Aeneas's eyes in the storm of Book I (113–117); the Lycians of south-western Asia Minor were Troy's allies in the Iliad. Leucaspis is named only here. 'Quos… vectos' is 'whom, carried' by sea, with 'simul', 'together', that is in company with Aeneas. 'Ab Troia' is 'from Troy' (the Latin Library prints 'a'). 'Obruit' is 'overwhelmed', with 'Auster', the South Wind, as subject, held back until the verb. 'Aqua' is an ablative of means with 'involvens', 'wrapping in water'; 'navemque virosque' has the double '-que', 'both ship and men'.

sentences.t:
Ecce gubernator sese Palinurus agebat,
qui Libyco nuper cursu, dum sidera servat,
exciderat puppi mediis effusus in undis.
sentences.l:
Look, the helmsman was making his way, Palinurus,
who on the Libyan lately voyage, while the stars he watched,
had fallen from the stern, flung out into the middle of the waves.
sentences.i: And now came the helmsman Palinurus, who not long before, on the voyage from Libya, had fallen from the stern while he was watching the stars, and been flung out into the open sea.
sentences.n: A new paragraph. 'Ecce' is 'look!', a sudden arrival. 'Sese… agebat' is 'was driving himself on', coming towards them. Palinurus's fall from the ship is the close of Book V. 'Libyco… cursu' is 'on the Libyan voyage', though in Book V he falls on the run from Sicily to Italy: it must mean the voyage that began in Libya, and readers have long counted it among the loose threads of a poem Virgil did not live to revise. 'Dum sidera servat' is 'while he watches the stars', 'dum' with the present indicative even in past time. 'Exciderat' is the pluperfect of 'excido', 'had fallen out'; 'puppi' is an ablative of separation, 'from the stern'. 'In… undis', with the ablative after a verb of motion, is a usage of verse: 'flung out (and lying) in the midst of the waves'. Palinurus is Virgil's Elpenor, the crewman of Odysseus who died in an accident before the descent and meets him first among the dead, begging burial (Odyssey 11.51–80).

sentences.t:
Hunc ubi vix multa maestum cognovit in umbra,
sic prior adloquitur:
sentences.l:
Him when hardly he recognised, sorrowful, in the thick shade,
thus first he addresses him:
sentences.i: When he had at last made him out in the thick gloom, sad as he was, Aeneas spoke to him first:
sentences.n: 'Hunc ubi… cognovit' is 'when he recognised him', the object put first. 'Vix' is 'hardly', 'with difficulty'. 'Multa… in umbra' is 'in the thick shade', with 'maestum', 'sorrowful', set between; 'multa' is 'much', 'dense'. 'Prior' is 'first', before the other could speak. 'Adloquitur' is Greenough's spelling of 'alloquitur', 'addresses', a deponent; the colon opens Aeneas's question.

sentences.t:
“Quis te, Palinure, deorum
eripuit nobis, medioque sub aequore mersit?
sentences.l:
“Who you, Palinurus, of the gods
snatched from us, and in the middle beneath the sea drowned?
sentences.i: “Which of the gods, Palinurus, took you from us and drowned you in the open sea?
sentences.n: The opening mark begins Aeneas's words, which run to 346. 'Quis… deorum' is 'which of the gods', framing the first line. 'Nobis' is a dative of separation, as often with verbs of taking away, 'snatched from us'. 'Medio sub aequore' is 'under mid-sea', the open water. 'Mersit' is 'sank', 'drowned'. So Odysseus asks Elpenor how he came to the darkness before him (Odyssey 11.57–58).

sentences.t: Dic age.
sentences.l: Tell me, come.
sentences.i: Tell me, come.
sentences.n: 'Age', 'come!', is an imperative of 'ago' used as an interjection to urge on another imperative, 'dic', 'tell'. Two words and a full stop.

sentences.t:
Namque mihi, fallax haud ante repertus,
hoc uno responso animum delusit Apollo,
qui fore te ponto incolumem, finesque canebat
venturum Ausonios.
sentences.l:
For to me, deceitful never before found,
by this one answer my mind has deceived Apollo,
who that you would be on the sea unharmed, and the borders was singing
that you would reach, Ausonian.
sentences.i: For Apollo, whom I never before found false, deceived me in this one answer, when he foretold that you would come through the sea unharmed and reach the shores of Ausonia.
sentences.n: 'Mihi… animum' is 'my mind', 'mihi' a dative of reference used instead of a possessive. 'Fallax haud ante repertus' is 'never before found deceitful', in apposition to Apollo, the subject held to the end of the line. 'Hoc uno responso' is 'by this one answer', an ablative of means. 'Qui… canebat' is 'who was singing', that is prophesying, oracles being given in verse. 'Fore' is the future infinitive of 'sum' ('futurum esse'), 'that you would be'; 'ponto' is 'on the sea', an ablative of place. 'Finesque… venturum Ausonios' is 'and that you would come to the Ausonian borders', 'venturum (esse)' with an accusative of goal and no preposition; 'finesque' is spelt 'finisque' in the Latin Library. Ausonia is a poetic name for Italy. No such oracle is reported earlier in the poem.

sentences.t: En haec promissa fides est?”
sentences.l: Is this the promised faith?”
sentences.i: Is this how he keeps his word?”
sentences.n: 'En' is 'look!', and here it gives the question an indignant edge, 'is this, then…?'. 'Haec promissa fides est?' is 'is this the promised faith?', that is, the promise made good. The closing mark ends Aeneas's question.

sentences.t:
Ille autem: “Neque te Phoebi cortina fefellit,
dux Anchisiade, nec me deus aequore mersit.
sentences.l:
He then: “Neither did Phoebus's cauldron deceive you,
leader, son of Anchises, nor did a god drown me in the sea.
sentences.i: And he replied: “Phoebus's oracle did not deceive you, my lord, son of Anchises, nor did any god drown me in the sea.
sentences.n: 'Ille autem' is 'and he', with the verb of speaking left out, as often. The opening mark begins Palinurus's speech, which runs to 371. 'Cortina' is the cauldron on the tripod at Delphi, where the priestess sat, and so 'the oracle' of Phoebus Apollo. 'Fefellit' is the perfect of 'fallo', 'deceive'. 'Anchisiade' is the vocative of the Greek patronymic 'Anchisiades', 'son of Anchises'. 'Nec me deus aequore mersit' answers 'quis… deorum… mersit' word for word. In Book V it was the god Sleep who pushed him overboard; Palinurus, who was asleep, may simply not know it, or this is another seam left unsmoothed.

sentences.t:
Namque gubernaclum multa vi forte revolsum,
cui datus haerebam custos cursusque regebam,
praecipitans traxi mecum.
sentences.l:
For the rudder, with great force by chance torn away,
to which, assigned as guardian, I was clinging and the course was ruling,
falling headlong I dragged with me.
sentences.i: For the helm was wrenched away with great force by some chance, and as I fell headlong I dragged it with me, the helm I clung to as its appointed keeper, steering our course.
sentences.n: 'Gubernaclum' is the shortened form of 'gubernaculum', 'steering-oar', 'helm', the object of 'traxi', held back to the third line. 'Revolsum' is Greenough's old spelling of 'revulsum', 'torn off', the participle of 'revello'; Book V (858) also has the helm torn away with him. 'Multa vi' is 'with much force', and 'forte' is 'by chance'. 'Cui… haerebam' is 'to which I was clinging', with 'datus… custos', 'given as its guardian', in apposition to the subject. 'Cursus regebam' is 'I was steering our courses'. 'Praecipitans' is 'falling headlong', an intransitive use of 'praecipito'.

sentences.t:
Maria aspera iuro
non ullum pro me tantum cepisse timorem,
quam tua ne, spoliata armis, excussa magistro,
deficeret tantis navis surgentibus undis.
sentences.l:
By the rough seas I swear
not any for myself so great to have taken fear,
as that your, stripped of its gear, shaken free of its master,
might fail, in such great rising waves, ship.
sentences.i: I swear by the cruel seas that I felt no fear for myself so great as my fear that your ship, robbed of its helm and its helmsman shaken off, might founder in those mountainous waves.
sentences.n: 'Maria aspera iuro' is 'I swear by the rough seas', 'iuro' with an accusative of what one swears by, as at 324. The accusative and infinitive follows with its subject 'me' left out: '(me) non ullum… tantum cepisse timorem', 'that I felt no fear so great'. 'Pro me' is 'for myself'. 'Quam' after 'tantum' is 'as', the comparison completed by the fear clause: 'ne… deficeret' is 'that it might fail', 'ne' with the subjunctive after the idea of fear. 'Tua… navis' frames two lines. 'Spoliata armis' is 'stripped of its gear', here the steering-oar, and 'excussa magistro' is 'with its master shaken out', both ablatives of separation. 'Tantis… surgentibus undis' is an ablative absolute, 'such great waves rising'.

sentences.t:
Tris Notus hibernas immensa per aequora noctes
vexit me violentus aqua; vix lumine quarto
prospexi Italiam summa sublimis ab unda.
sentences.l:
Three the South Wind wintry over the boundless seas nights
carried me, violent, on the water; scarcely at the fourth light
I caught sight of Italy, from a wave's top lifted high.
sentences.i: For three stormy nights the South Wind drove me furiously over the endless sea; at the fourth dawn, lifted high on the crest of a wave, I could just make out Italy.
sentences.n: 'Tris… hibernas… noctes' frames the first line, an accusative of duration, 'for three wintry nights'; 'tris' is Greenough's old form of the accusative plural 'tres'. 'Hibernas' is 'wintry', that is stormy. 'Notus' is the Greek name of the South Wind. 'Violentus' is an adjective where English uses an adverb, 'violently'; 'aqua' is an ablative, 'on the water'. 'Lumine quarto' is 'at the fourth light', the fourth dawn, an ablative of time. 'Prospexi' is 'looked out on', 'caught sight of'. 'Summa… ab unda' is 'from the top of a wave', with 'sublimis', 'raised aloft', between.

sentences.t: Paulatim adnabam terrae;
sentences.l: Little by little I was swimming to land;
sentences.i: Little by little I was swimming in to land;
sentences.n: 'Adnabam' is Greenough's spelling of 'annabam', the imperfect of 'adno', 'swim towards', describing a slow effort still going on. 'Terrae' is a dative with the compound verb, 'to the land'.

sentences.t:
iam tuta tenebam,
ni gens crudelis madida cum veste gravatum
prensantemque uncis manibus capita aspera montis
ferro invasisset, praedamque ignara putasset.
sentences.l:
already safety I was holding,
had not a people cruel, with my soaked clothing weighed down,
and clutching with hooked hands the rough peaks of a cliff,
with steel attacked me, and as plunder in ignorance had thought me.
sentences.i: I was already within reach of safety, had not a savage people fallen on me with the sword as I clutched with crooked fingers at the jagged rocks of a headland, weighed down by my sodden clothes, and in their ignorance taken me for a prize.
sentences.n: 'Iam tuta tenebam' is 'I was already holding safety', 'tuta' a neuter plural, 'safe places'. The condition is contrary to fact in past time, 'ni… invasisset… putasset', 'had not… attacked… and thought', but the main clause stands in the imperfect indicative instead of the subjunctive, a vivid turn: he was as good as safe. 'Gens crudelis' is 'a cruel people', natives of the coast. 'Gravatum' and 'prensantem' agree with an unstated 'me': 'weighed down', 'madida cum veste', 'with my wet clothing', and 'grasping'. 'Uncis manibus' is 'with hooked hands', fingers bent like claws; 'capita aspera montis' is 'the rough heads of a cliff'. 'Ferro' is 'with steel'. 'Praedam… putasset' is 'had thought (me) plunder', 'praedam' a predicate accusative; 'putasset' is the shortened pluperfect for 'putavisset'. 'Ignara' agrees with 'gens', 'not knowing' who he was.

sentences.t: Nunc me fluctus habet, versantque in litore venti.
sentences.l: Now me the wave holds, and they toss me on the shore, the winds.
sentences.i: Now the waves have me, and the winds roll me to and fro along the shore.
sentences.n: 'Fluctus' is 'the wave', the sea. 'Versant' is 'turn over and over'; 'in litore' is 'on the shore', in the surf. His body lies unburied at the water's edge, which is why he is on this bank. A plain line after the long sentence before it, its two verbs present: this is still going on.

sentences.t:
Quod te per caeli iucundum lumen et auras,
per genitorem oro, per spes surgentis Iuli,
eripe me his, invicte, malis: aut tu mihi terram
inice, namque potes, portusque require Velinos;
sentences.l:
Wherefore you by the sky's pleasant light and its airs,
by your father I beg, by the hopes of rising Iulus,
snatch me from these, unconquered one, ills: or you on me earth
throw, for you can, and seek out the harbours of Velia;
sentences.i: So I beg you, by the sweet light of heaven and the air you breathe, by your father, by your hopes in the growing Iulus, save me, unconquered one, from this misery: either throw earth over me yourself — you can — and look for the harbour of Velia;
sentences.n: 'Quod' opens an earnest appeal, 'and so', 'wherefore'; it is an old adverbial accusative, 'as to which'. 'Te… oro' is 'I beg you', with three oaths in 'per': 'per caeli iucundum lumen et auras', 'by the pleasant light of the sky and the airs', the things of the living world which he has lost; 'per genitorem', Anchises; 'per spes surgentis Iuli', 'by your hopes in growing Iulus', Aeneas's son. 'Eripe me his… malis' is 'snatch me from these troubles', 'his… malis' an ablative of separation round the vocative 'invicte'. 'Mihi terram inice' is 'throw earth on me': a handful of earth scattered on a body was a burial in law and religion. The 'i' of 'inice' after the prefix is consonantal, 'in-jice'. 'Require' is 'look for'. 'Portus… Velinos' is 'the harbour of Velia', a Greek town on the Lucanian coast near the cape, founded long after Aeneas's time, as ancient readers already noted.

sentences.t:
aut tu, si qua via est, si quam tibi diva creatrix
ostendit—neque enim, credo, sine numine divom
flumina tanta paras Stygiamque innare paludem—
da dextram misero, et tecum me tolle per undas,
sedibus ut saltem placidis in morte quiescam.”
sentences.l:
or you, if there is any way, if any you your goddess mother
shows — for not, I believe, without the will of the gods
such great rivers you are preparing and the Stygian marsh to sail —
give your right hand to a wretched man, and with you take me over the waves,
that in a resting-place at least, a peaceful one, in death I may rest.”
sentences.i: or else, if there is a way, if your goddess mother shows you one — for I do not think you are setting out to sail such mighty rivers and the marsh of Styx without the gods' blessing — give your hand to a man in misery and take me with you over the water, so that at least in death I may find a quiet resting-place.”
sentences.n: 'Aut tu' answers 'aut tu' at 365, the second of two choices. 'Si qua via est' is 'if there is any way', 'qua' the indefinite after 'si', and 'si quam' is 'if any (way)'; 'diva creatrix' is 'the goddess who bore you', Venus. Greenough's dashes enclose a parenthesis: 'neque enim… paras' is 'for you are not, I think, preparing'. 'Divom' is the old genitive plural, 'of the gods', and 'numine' is 'divine will'. 'Innare' is 'to swim upon', 'to sail', taking the accusative 'flumina tanta Stygiamque paludem'. 'Da dextram misero' is 'give your right hand to a wretched man', 'misero' a dative. 'Tolle' is 'take up'. 'Sedibus ut… placidis… quiescam' is a purpose clause with 'ut' put second; 'saltem' is 'at least'. The closing mark ends Palinurus's plea, which follows Elpenor's to Odysseus in Odyssey 11 (66–78): remember me, burn and bury me by the sea.

sentences.t: Talia fatus erat, coepit cum talia vates:
sentences.l: Such things he had spoken, when began such things the seer:
sentences.i: So he had spoken, when the prophetess began:
sentences.n: A new paragraph. 'Talia fatus erat, coepit cum…' is the inverted 'cum' again: the main clause gives the moment, the 'cum' clause in the indicative the next event; 'cum' stands second in its clause. 'Fatus erat' is the pluperfect of the deponent 'for'. 'Talia… talia' is 'such things… such things', the repetition marking speech answering speech. 'Coepit' is 'began', with 'to speak' understood. 'Vates' is the Sibyl.

sentences.t: “Unde haec, o Palinure, tibi tam dira cupido?
sentences.l: “Whence this, O Palinurus, to you so dread desire?
sentences.i: “Palinurus, where did this terrible longing come from?
sentences.n: The opening mark begins the Sibyl's reply, which runs to 381. 'Unde' is 'from where?'. 'Tibi' is a dative of possession, 'to you is this desire'. 'Dira' is 'dreadful', 'ill-omened', because the wish breaks divine law. 'Cupido', 'desire', is feminine here, as normally when it is not the god Cupid.

sentences.t:
Tu Stygias inhumatus aquas amnemque severum
Eumenidum aspicies, ripamve iniussus adibis?
sentences.l:
You, unburied, the Stygian waters and the river grim
of the Eumenides will look upon, or the bank unbidden will approach?
sentences.i: Will you, unburied, look upon the waters of Styx and the stern river of the Furies, or come to the bank unbidden?
sentences.n: A question with no question-word, spoken in indignant surprise: 'tu… aspicies…?', 'you will see…?'. 'Inhumatus' is 'unburied', the whole point. 'Amnem… severum Eumenidum' is 'the stern river of the Eumenides', the Furies (named 'the Kindly Ones' to avoid ill-omen), who have their seat in the underworld. 'Iniussus' is 'unbidden', without the leave of the gods. '-ve' is 'or'.

sentences.t: Desine fata deum flecti sperare precando.
sentences.l: Cease the fates of the gods to be bent to hope by praying.
sentences.i: Give up hoping that pleading will turn the gods' decrees from their course.
sentences.n: 'Desine' is 'stop', with the infinitive 'sperare'. 'Fata deum… flecti' is an accusative and infinitive after 'sperare', 'that the fates of the gods are bent'; 'deum' is the old genitive plural again, and 'flecti' is the present passive infinitive (after 'spero' a future would be usual; the present makes it a general truth). 'Precando' is the ablative of the gerund, 'by praying', 'by entreaty'.

sentences.t: Sed cape dicta memor, duri solatia casus.
sentences.l: But take my words, mindful, a comfort for your hard fate.
sentences.i: But take what I say to heart, as a comfort in your hard fortune.
sentences.n: 'Cape dicta memor' is 'take my words remembering', 'memor' an adjective where English uses a phrase, 'and keep them in mind'. 'Duri solatia casus' is in apposition to 'dicta', 'consolations of a hard fall', the genitive 'casus' meaning his misfortune; Greenough's 'solatia' is spelt 'solacia' in the Latin Library.

sentences.t:
Nam tua finitimi, longe lateque per urbes
prodigiis acti caelestibus, ossa piabunt,
et statuent tumulum, et tumulo sollemnia mittent,
aeternumque locus Palinuri nomen habebit.”
sentences.l:
For your neighbours, far and wide through their cities
by portents driven heavenly, bones will appease,
and they will set up a mound, and to the mound solemn rites will send,
and for ever the place Palinurus's name will have.”
sentences.i: For the peoples who live nearby, in cities far and wide, driven by portents from heaven, will make atonement to your bones; they will raise a mound and pay it yearly offerings, and the place will bear the name of Palinurus for ever.”
sentences.n: 'Tua… ossa' is 'your bones', the object of 'piabunt', framing two lines. 'Finitimi' is 'the neighbours', the peoples of the coast. 'Longe lateque' is 'far and wide'. 'Prodigiis acti caelestibus' is 'driven by heavenly portents', signs of divine anger; ancient commentators told of a plague in Lucania, ended when an oracle bade the people appease the ghost of Palinurus. 'Piabunt' is 'will appease', make expiation to. 'Tumulum' is a burial mound; 'sollemnia' are 'solemn rites', yearly offerings to the dead, 'mittent' being 'will send' them. 'Aeternum' is an adverbial accusative, 'for ever'. Cape Palinuro on the Lucanian coast still bears the name, as Cape Misenum bears Misenus's (234–235). The closing mark ends the Sibyl's speech.

sentences.t:
His dictis curae emotae, pulsusque parumper
corde dolor tristi:
sentences.l:
By these words his cares were removed, and driven for a little while
from his heart was the grief, sad heart:
sentences.i: At these words his cares were lifted, and for a little while the grief was driven from his sorrowing heart:
sentences.n: 'His dictis' is an ablative of cause or an ablative absolute, 'by these words'. 'Emotae' and 'pulsus' have their 'sunt' and 'est' left out. 'Parumper' is 'for a short while'. 'Corde… tristi' is an ablative of separation, 'from his sad heart', with 'dolor' set between the noun and its adjective; the colon leads to the reason.

sentences.t: gaudet cognomine terrae.
sentences.l: he rejoices in the name of the land.
sentences.i: he takes joy in a land that will bear his name.
sentences.n: 'Cognomine terrae' is 'in the land's surname', the name the place will take from him ('terrae' a genitive, or perhaps a dative, 'the name given to the land'); 'gaudeo' takes an ablative of cause. The Latin Library prints 'terra', which changes the construction: either 'the land rejoices in his name', 'terra' becoming the subject, or 'he rejoices in the land of the same name', with 'cognomine' the ablative of the adjective 'cognominis', agreeing with 'terra'.

sentences.t: Ergo iter inceptum peragunt fluvioque propinquant.
sentences.l: So the journey begun they carry through and to the river draw near.
sentences.i: So they continued the journey they had begun and drew near the river.
sentences.n: A new paragraph. 'Ergo' is 'so', 'accordingly', resuming the story after the meeting. 'Iter inceptum' is 'the journey begun'. 'Peragunt' is 'carry through', 'complete'. 'Fluvio' is a dative after 'propinquant', 'draw near to the river'.

sentences.t:
Navita quos iam inde ut Stygia prospexit ab unda
per tacitum nemus ire pedemque advertere ripae,
sic prior adgreditur dictis, atque increpat ultro:
sentences.l:
The boatman, when them already from there, from the Stygian, he saw from the water
through the silent grove going and turning their step to the bank,
thus first he accosts them with words, and chides them unprovoked:
sentences.i: The boatman, when he caught sight of them from his place on the Stygian water, coming through the silent wood and turning their steps towards the bank, spoke to them first and rebuked them before they said a word:
sentences.n: 'Navita' is Charon again. 'Quos' is the object of 'prospexit' and the subject of the two infinitives, 'that they were going… and turning'; it is a relative used to link the sentence to the last ('and when he saw them'). 'Iam inde' is 'already from there', explained by 'Stygia… ab unda', 'from the Stygian water'. 'Ut' with the perfect is 'when'. 'Pedem advertere ripae' is 'to turn the foot to the bank', 'ripae' a dative of direction. 'Prior' is 'first'. 'Adgreditur' is Greenough's spelling of 'aggreditur', 'approaches', 'accosts', a deponent; 'dictis' is 'with words'. 'Ultro' is 'unprovoked', 'of his own accord', before anyone has spoken to him. The colon opens his challenge.

sentences.t:
“Quisquis es, armatus qui nostra ad flumina tendis,
fare age, quid venias, iam istinc, et comprime gressum.
sentences.l:
“Whoever you are, who armed to our rivers make your way,
speak, come, why you come, from there now, and check your step.
sentences.i: “Whoever you are who come armed to my river, say what you want here — from where you stand — and come no nearer.
sentences.n: The opening mark begins Charon's speech, which runs to 397. 'Quisquis es' is 'whoever you are'. 'Armatus' is 'armed': the Sibyl told Aeneas to draw his sword at 260, and he drew it on the monsters at 290. 'Nostra… flumina' is 'our rivers', the plural of majesty; 'tendis' is 'you make your way'. 'Fare age' is 'come, speak', 'fare' the imperative of 'for' with 'age' urging it on, as 'dic age' at 343. 'Quid venias' is an indirect question in the subjunctive, 'why you come'. 'Iam istinc' is 'at once, from there', 'istinc' being 'from where you are'. 'Comprime gressum' is 'restrain your step'.

sentences.t: Umbrarum hic locus est, somni noctisque soporae;
sentences.l: Of shades this place is, of sleep and of night drowsy;
sentences.i: This is the place of the shades, of sleep and of slumberous night;
sentences.n: 'Umbrarum… locus' is 'the place of shades', a possessive genitive, followed by two more, 'somni noctisque soporae'. 'Soporus' is a rare adjective, 'sleep-bringing', 'drowsy'.

sentences.t: corpora viva nefas Stygia vectare carina.
sentences.l: living bodies it is unlawful in the Stygian to carry keel.
sentences.i: it is forbidden to carry living bodies in the boat of Styx.
sentences.n: 'Nefas (est)' is 'it is against divine law', with the infinitive 'vectare' as subject. 'Vectare' is the frequentative of 'veho', 'to carry'. 'Carina' is 'keel', standing for the whole boat (the part for the whole), an ablative of means or place; 'Stygia… carina' frames the end of the line.

sentences.t:
Nec vero Alciden me sum laetatus euntem
accepisse lacu, nec Thesea Pirithoumque,
dis quamquam geniti atque invicti viribus essent.
sentences.l:
Nor indeed Alcides was I glad myself, as he went,
to have received on the lake, nor Theseus and Pirithous,
though from gods they were born and unconquered in strength they were.
sentences.i: And indeed I had no joy of taking Alcides aboard on the lake when he went his way, nor Theseus and Pirithous, though they were sons of gods and their strength was unconquered.
sentences.n: 'Nec vero' is 'nor in truth'. 'Alciden' is a Greek accusative: Alcides, 'grandson of Alceus', is Hercules. 'Sum laetatus' (the deponent 'laetor', 'rejoice') takes an accusative and infinitive, 'me… accepisse', 'that I received', with the subject 'me' expressed. 'Euntem' is 'going', on his way down. 'Lacu' is 'on the lake', the marshy river, an ablative of place. 'Thesea' and 'Pirithoum' are Greek accusatives. 'Dis… geniti' is 'born of gods', 'dis' an ablative of origin: Hercules was the son of Jupiter, Pirithous by some accounts too, Theseus of Neptune. 'Quamquam' with the subjunctive 'essent' is a usage of poets and later prose, where Cicero would have the indicative. 'Viribus' is an ablative of respect, 'in strength'.

sentences.t:
Tartareum ille manu custodem in vincla petivit,
ipsius a solio regis, traxitque trementem;
sentences.l:
The Tartarean that one by hand the guardian into chains sought,
from the very throne of the king, and dragged him off trembling;
sentences.i: The one came to put the watchdog of Tartarus in chains with his own hands, and dragged him away cowering from the very throne of the king;
sentences.n: 'Ille' is 'the former', Hercules. 'Tartareum… custodem' frames the line, 'the guardian of Tartarus', Cerberus, the many-headed dog of the underworld; fetching him up to the light was the last of Hercules' labours, told by his own shade in Odyssey 11 (623–626). 'Manu' is 'by hand', by force. 'In vincla petivit' is 'sought for chains', that is went for him to chain him; 'vincla' is the shortened form of 'vincula'. 'Ipsius a solio regis' is 'from the throne of the king himself', Dis, with 'a' placed after 'ipsius'. 'Trementem' is 'trembling', Cerberus's terror.

sentences.t: hi dominam Ditis thalamo deducere adorti.”
sentences.l: these the mistress from Dis's chamber to lead away attempted.”
sentences.i: the others set out to carry off the queen from the bridal chamber of Dis.”
sentences.n: 'Hi' is 'these', 'the latter', Theseus and Pirithous. 'Adorti' (with 'sunt' left out) is 'undertook', 'attempted', from the deponent 'adorior', with the infinitive 'deducere'. 'Deducere' is the word for leading a bride to her new home, used here with bitter point: Pirithous meant to take Proserpina, 'domina', 'the mistress' of the house, for his own wife. 'Thalamo' is an ablative of separation, 'from the bedchamber'. The attempt failed, and both were held fast below; Theseus will be seen later in this book, sitting for ever (617–618). The closing mark ends Charon's speech.
